facts.text: Turner, Maine, was granted in 1690 to Captain Joseph Sylvester for his service in King William's War, and was first called Sylvester‑Canada.
In 1786, Sylvester‑Canada was renamed for Reverend Charles Turner and incorporated, becoming an agricultural community that grew corn, apples, and early manufacturing.
Turner’s 19th‑century chair industry, led by the North Turner Chair Factory—rebuilt in 1886 as the Washburn Chair Company—pioneered willow chair production in Maine.
Samuel Blake built Turner’s first sawmill and gristmill on the Nezinscot River in 1775; it was destroyed by a freshet in 1785 and rebuilt the next year.
Turner’s historic buildings and landmarks, many listed on the National Register of Historic Places, showcase the town’s rich architectural heritage.
Turner encompasses the villages of Turner, Turner Center, and North Turner, each reflecting different aspects of the town’s rural character.
